title: At home here
hook: Odysseus wept for home on Calypso's island; Heracles was at home anywhere

segments.voice: Yesterday: in its season, the fig that comes and goes. Did you thank someone for the season they were in your life? Day four hundred twenty-four.

A man sits on a rock at the edge of the sea, staring at the horizon, crying. He's on a beautiful island. A goddess loves him and has offered him a life without death. He doesn't care. Day after day he goes down to the shore and weeps for a rocky little kingdom he hasn't seen in years. That's Odysseus, in book five of Homer's Odyssey, on Calypso's island. Epictetus picked it up and asked an awkward question about it. Today: at home here.
screen: `A MAN ON A ROCK, CRYING.` → `CALYPSO'S ISLAND.` → `AT HOME HERE.`

segments.voice: First, the weeping. Epictetus, in that same long chapter of book three, asks whether we should take Homer at his word in everything. If Odysseus really sat and wept like that, he says, then he was unhappy, not living well. Homer may have told it that way, but a person who can only be happy in one spot on the map has handed their happiness to geography. Epictetus isn't mocking homesickness. He's asking where we've put our peace. Second, the other hero. Then he turns to Heracles. In the old stories Heracles traveled the whole known world on his labors, clearing out cruelty and lawlessness wherever he went. Epictetus says he made friends in every place, had children in more than one land, and left them without groaning, not because he didn't love them, but because he believed every human being was his kin, and Zeus the father of all. Third, the old phrase. It's the citizen of the world we met on the day of names, who am I here. Diogenes the Cynic, asked where he was from, is said to have answered: I'm a citizen of the world, a kosmopolitēs. Fourth, what it isn't. It isn't a rule against missing home. Epictetus doesn't say don't love your city, your street, your mother's kitchen. He says don't make them the only place you can stand up straight. Wherever there are people, sky and a chance to act well, there is work for you to do. A hospital waiting room, a new apartment, a strange city at night. You can be at home there too.
screen: `ODYSSEUS WEEPS ON THE ROCK.` · `HERACLES IS AT HOME ANYWHERE.` · `A CITIZEN OF THE WORLD.` · `LOVE HOME; DON'T NEED ONLY IT.` · then, large: `AT HOME HERE.`

segments.voice: Wherever you are right now, a bedroom, a bus, a break room, let your eyes move slowly around it. Notice the light. Notice one thing someone made with their hands: a chair, a window, a cup. Feel what's holding you up, the seat or the floor. Breathe in this air, the air of exactly here. And quietly tell yourself: this, too, is a place where a person can live well. You don't have to love it. Just let yourself stand in it, at home for these two minutes. The bell holds the time.
At home here. The Stoic picture of Heracles, kin to every person in every land, set against Odysseus weeping on his rock: peace that doesn't depend on one spot on the map. Today's word.

Your line: at home here. The next time you're somewhere you'd rather not be, a line, an office, a waiting room, say it once under your breath and look for one good thing to do there. Day four hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Stoic writers, Epictetus among them, speak of being citizens of the world, and some practitioners make a habit of settling into wherever they are, treating any place as a place where they can act well.

fork.setup: you're Odysseus. a goddess offers you an endless, easy life on her island, far from home. what do you do?
options: sit on the shore every day and weep.
build a raft and sail home.
fork.reveal: in book five he weeps on the shore for years, until the gods send word to let him go. Epictetus asks whether that weeping was living well.

original.note: Greek: a citizen (polites) of the cosmos; Diogenes the Cynic is said to have called himself one.

trapdoor: what you thought: home is where your stuff is.
what it means: Epictetus holds up Heracles, at home everywhere, against Odysseus weeping on his rock for one place.
what a scholar hears: Epictetus treats Homer's weeping Odysseus as a moral example to question, not a hero to copy, a bold move with Homer.

notes: Discourses 3.24: Odysseus weeping on Calypso's island and Heracles traveling, with children in many places, leaving them without grief, believing Zeus father of all; paraphrased. Confirm section numbers (approx. 3.24.13–21).
Epictetus' verdict on Odysseus is softened in the script ('in that moment he wasn't living well'); the Greek is sharper (if he wept, he was unhappy / not good). Confirm.
Odyssey 5: Calypso offers immortality (5.135–136, 5.209); Odysseus weeps on the shore (5.81–84, 5.151–158). Confirm line numbers.
Diogenes Laertius 6.63: 'kosmopolites'. 'Said to have used the word first' is the common claim; confirm or soften.
'The Stoic idea we met in year one' refers to the cosmopolitan theme in year one's Stoic days; confirm a matching day exists.
